passage: In Rania's class in Madrid, a boy announced that kids who drink energy drinks score better in football trials, because "all the best players on the team drink them." Javier nodded along. Rania didn't. At lunch she said, "Maybe the best players just train more and buy drinks with their pocket money. The drink isn't the reason." Javier looked annoyed. "The coach even said they help." "Did he show anything? Or just say it?" Rania asked. That evening Javier searched for proper studies and found none that tested it. He grudgingly texted her: "Ok, no proof 🙄 still tasty." Rania sent back a thumbs-up and a note to check with the coach about the claim.

qa.q: What did the boy claim about energy drinks?
qa.a: He claimed that kids who drink them score better in football trials because all the best players drink them.

qa.q: How can you tell Javier was reluctant to change his mind?
qa.a: He looked annoyed and pointed to the coach, and even his text admitting there was no proof sounded grudging.

qa.q: What did Rania do that others could copy when they hear a claim?
qa.a: She asked whether something else could explain the pattern and whether the coach showed evidence or only said it.

qa.q: How might the boy who made the claim feel if Rania questioned him in class?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed or defensive, so a calm question in private may have gone down better than calling him out.

grounding: It shows teens questioning a claim that confuses correlation with causation and relies on authority rather than evidence.

passage: In the physics lab, Swati's group had to test whether heavier balls roll down the ramp faster. Aparna, the topper, said, "Of course they do, my brother said so." Swati wasn't so sure. "Let's just time it." They rolled a steel ball and a marble five times each. The results were almost the same, and the small differences kept changing. Aparna frowned at the notebook. "Maybe we did it wrong." Swati suggested they try ten more times, and change who held the stopwatch. The results still matched. Aparna crossed out her prediction and wrote the real numbers. "My brother's going to argue," she said. Swati grinned. "Show him the notebook."

qa.q: How many times did they roll each ball at first?
qa.a: They rolled each ball five times.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she frowned at the notebook?
qa.a: She was uneasy and a bit reluctant, because the results went against what she had been sure of and what her brother had said.

qa.q: Why was repeating the test and changing the stopwatch holder a good idea?
qa.a: It checked whether the result was due to chance or one person's timing, so the conclusion rested on stronger evidence.

qa.q: How might Aparna's brother react to the notebook?
qa.a: He might argue at first, but the repeated measurements give Aparna evidence that is harder to dismiss than just his opinion.

grounding: It shows teens judging a claim by testing it rather than trusting who said it.

passage:
Dear Chinmay,
You forwarded me that message again, the one saying people who eat breakfast early live longer, "backed by doctors." I know you mean well. But I read the actual study. They only found early eaters tend to live longer. It didn't prove breakfast does it. Maybe early eaters sleep earlier, walk more, or just have calmer jobs. And "backed by doctors" didn't name a single doctor.
I'm not saying breakfast is bad. Eat it if you like it! I'm saying the message sounds more sure than the study is. If you're worried about health, ask your own doctor.
Also please stop forwarding stuff to the family group at 6 am. Nani's phone buzzes and wakes her up 😅
Your brother,
Omkar

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: It claimed people who eat breakfast early live longer and said it was backed by doctors.

qa.q: What does Omkar's line "I know you mean well" show about his feelings?
qa.a: He wants to correct Chinmay without hurting him, showing care for his brother even while disagreeing.

qa.q: What made Omkar's reply to the message sensible?
qa.a: He read the actual study, pointed out other explanations, noticed no doctor was named, and suggested asking a real doctor instead of trusting forwards.

qa.q: If you were Chinmay, how might you feel reading this email?
qa.a: You might feel a little corrected, but the warm tone and the joke about Nani's phone would make it easier to accept. 🙂

grounding: A teen's email to his brother separates correlation from causation and questions a claim resting on vague authority.

passage: So Suraj, you know Rakesh sir, the one who's always on those study videos? He said students who study with music score higher. Everyone in our class started repeating it. Even my cousin put on headphones while doing trigonometry. I got curious and found the survey he quoted. It was twenty students from one coaching centre. Twenty! And they just asked them if they liked music and what their marks were. It didn't test anything. Maybe kids who can afford their own quiet room with speakers also have tutors. That's correlation, not causation, right? I'm not saying music is bad. I'm saying a famous person repeating something ten times doesn't make it evidence. Now I ask: how big was the study, and what did they actually measure?

qa.q: How many students were in the survey Rakesh sir quoted?
qa.a: Twenty students from one coaching centre.

qa.q: What made the narrator curious enough to look up the survey?
qa.a: Everyone was repeating the claim, even the narrator's cousin, and the narrator wanted to know if it was really true.

qa.q: What questions does the narrator now use to judge a claim?
qa.a: How big the study was and what it actually measured, rather than trusting who said it.

qa.q: How might the narrator's classmates react to these findings?
qa.a: Some might feel silly for copying the idea, while others might defend the famous teacher out of habit.

grounding: A teen explains judging a claim by the quality of evidence and spotting correlation versus causation, not authority.

passage: I'm Ganga, Tushar's older sister. For the science fair, he wanted to test whether plants grow better with music, because his friend's uncle swore by it and everyone in the building repeated it. First he put a pot beside the radio on the sunny windowsill and another in the corner. The windowsill plant grew taller. He was thrilled. Then he stopped and stared at them for ages. I don't know what went through his head. The next day he moved both plants to the same windowsill, same water, same soil, and played music to only one. Three weeks later they were almost the same height. He wrote on his chart: 'Sunlight, not songs?' His teacher gave him a special mention.

qa.q: Where did Tushar first place the plant with the radio?
qa.a: On the sunny windowsill.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt as he stared at the plants for ages?
qa.a: He may have gone from thrilled to doubtful, noticing the windowsill plant also had more sunlight, though Ganga isn't sure.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's second experiment better than the first?
qa.a: He kept sunlight, water and soil the same so only the music differed, which gave fairer evidence.

qa.q: How might the friend's uncle respond to Tushar's result?
qa.a: He might be surprised or unwilling to believe it, since he had repeated the claim with such confidence.

grounding: An observer describes a teen testing a repeated claim and separating correlation from cause.

passage:
Monday: A forwarded message in Vidya's class group said: Students who have a study lamp score 20% higher! Buy yours today! Vidya, fifteen, almost believed it. Her brother Siddharth said, “Maybe. But why?”
Wednesday: Vidya looked for the study. It was done by the lamp company. It found that students with lamps scored higher. But it didn't say whether those families also had quiet rooms, tuition, or more books.
Saturday: In class, she presented it. “The lamp might help a little. But the families who buy lamps may also have other things that help. That's correlation, not proof the lamp causes it.”
The teacher asked her to write it for the school magazine.

qa.q: Who did the study about study lamps?
qa.a: The lamp company.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel on Monday when she saw the message?
qa.a: She felt tempted to believe it, almost convinced.

qa.q: What questions helped Vidya judge the claim?
qa.a: Who did the study and whether other things, like quiet rooms or tuition, could explain the higher scores.

qa.q: How did Siddharth help Vidya think more carefully?
qa.a: He asked “why?” instead of simply accepting the claim.

grounding: Over a week a fifteen-year-old learns to separate correlation from causation in a sales claim.

passage:
Himani, you're laughing at your Dadu's lucky shirt? Let your Gurleen Bua tell you a story.
When I was sixteen, our village cricket team was sure that red socks made us win. My father wore red socks to every match. Everyone said, “See? We won again!”
I was curious. For a whole season, I kept a notebook: socks, weather, which bowler played, who won the toss. At the end, I counted.
With red socks: we won half the matches. Without: also half. But when our fast bowler Gurnam played, we won nearly every time.
I showed my father. He was quiet, then laughed. “So the socks don't bowl.” He still wore them, but we started paying Gurnam's bus fare.

qa.q: What did young Gurleen record in her notebook?
qa.a: Socks, weather, which bowler played and who won the toss.

qa.q: How did Gurleen's father feel when she showed him the results?
qa.a: He was quiet, perhaps surprised, then amused, laughing about the socks.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped the team, and why?
qa.a: Paying Gurnam's bus fare, because the evidence showed he, not the socks, was linked with winning.

qa.q: How might Gurnam have felt when the team started paying his bus fare?
qa.a: He probably felt valued and proud that his bowling was recognised.

grounding: An aunt tells how, as a teenager, she used evidence to test a lucky belief.

passage:
The science fair was the next morning, and at 9 p.m. Yusuf and Vikas, both sixteen, were finishing their poster: Plants grow taller with music!
Their data looked great. The three pots next to the speaker had grown taller than the three by the door.
Then Yusuf stopped. “Wait. The speaker was by the window.”
Vikas groaned. “So they got more sun too.”
“We can't say it's the music.”
They had no time to redo the experiment. Vikas wanted to leave the poster as it was.
Yusuf crossed out the title and wrote: Did music or sunlight help? We don't know yet. Underneath, he added: Next time: same light, only music different.
At the fair, the judge stopped at their table longest.

qa.q: Where was the speaker?
qa.a: By the window.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when he realised the plants also got more sun?
qa.a: He felt worried and uneasy, but honest enough to change the claim.

qa.q: What was the right thing to do with the poster, and why?
qa.a: Change the title to say they didn't know yet, because sunlight could explain the result.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel about the change?
qa.a: He may feel frustrated at first, but relieved when the judge spends the longest at their table.

grounding: Under time pressure two sixteen-year-olds recognise a confounding factor and revise their claim honestly.

passage:
The ad on the Mumbai bus stop said: "Students who drink BrainBoost score higher!" There was a smiling topper with a trophy.
Madhav nudged Farida. "Maybe I should drink it before my exam."
Farida squinted. "Who says they score higher? The company?"
"Probably."
"And maybe kids who drink it have parents who can afford tuition too. So is it the drink or the tuition?"
Madhav thought. "So they go together, but the drink might not cause it."
"Exactly. Correlation isn't causation. Sir said so in science."
Madhav looked at the smiling topper again. "Still, the trophy looks nice."
Farida laughed. "Study for the trophy, not the drink."

qa.q: What did the bus stop ad say?
qa.a: "Students who drink BrainBoost score higher!"

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he thought about drinking it before his exam?
qa.a: Madhav felt hopeful and a bit tempted by the promise.

qa.q: What question did Farida ask that helped Madhav think better?
qa.a: She asked whether something else, like tuition, could explain the scores instead of the drink.

qa.q: How does Farida see the advert's claim?
qa.a: Farida is doubtful because the company made the claim and it confuses things that go together with causes.

grounding: A teen explains to a friend why a drink ad confuses correlation with causation.

passage:
"Did you see this forward?" said Hansa, holding out her phone. "Kids who eat breakfast get better marks. So I'm eating breakfast before every test."
Neelam read it. "It says 'studies show'. Which studies?"
"It doesn't say."
"And maybe kids who eat breakfast also sleep on time and have calmer mornings. That could be the real reason."
"So breakfast doesn't help?"
"It might. But the forward doesn't prove it. And it's from someone called 'Health Tips 4U'."
Hansa laughed. "Okay, that's not a scientist."
"Eat breakfast because it's good for you anyway. Just don't trust a forward because it's shared a hundred times."

qa.q: What was the forward from?
qa.a: Someone called 'Health Tips 4U'.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she laughed?
qa.a: Hansa felt amused and a little embarrassed at believing the forward so quickly.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time a forward says "studies show"?
qa.a: She could check which studies, who wrote it, and whether something else could explain the link.

qa.q: How does Neelam see forwards shared many times?
qa.a: Neelam thinks being shared a lot doesn't make something true.

grounding: Two teens question a forwarded message's claim about breakfast and marks.

passage:
In Class 8, I believed my blue pen was lucky. Every time I used it, I got good marks. I was sure the pen caused it.
My friend Hrithik laughed at me. "Did you also study more on those days?"
I got annoyed. "It's the pen."
So Hrithik said, "Test it. Next test, study the same but use a different pen."
I did. I used a black pen, and studied just as hard. I got the same marks.
I felt a bit silly. Now, when someone says "this caused that," I think of my blue pen. I'm Dhruv, and I still have it, but only because it writes smoothly.

qa.q: What colour was the pen Dhruv thought was lucky?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when getting annoyed at Hrithik?
qa.a: Dhruv felt defensive and irritated about the lucky pen being questioned.

qa.q: What did Hrithik suggest that turned Dhruv's belief into a test?
qa.a: Hrithik suggested changing only the pen while studying the same, which showed the pen didn't cause the marks.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when Dhruv gets the same marks?
qa.a: Hrithik is likely amused and pleased that the test proved the point.

grounding: A young person recalls testing a belief that a lucky pen caused good marks.

passage:
Science teacher's note, Class 9, 12 August (Bhavna)
Ujjwal announced today that his "lucky blue socks" make him score higher, because he wore them for his three best tests. Half the class agreed they'd seen it.
Instead of arguing, I asked the class to check. What else happened on those three days? Ujjwal thought. All three were Mondays, after quiet Sundays at home. He also admitted he'd revised more for those tests because they were chapters he liked.
We drew a chart: socks, sleep, revision, topic, marks. The pattern with revision was clearer than with socks.
Ujjwal laughed, a bit embarrassed. "But I'm still wearing them." Fine by me. The point is he now asks what else changed. Next week: I'll ask each student to test one "lucky" belief.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal claim about his blue socks?
qa.a: He said his lucky blue socks make him score higher, because he wore them for his three best tests.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when the chart showed revision mattered more?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt a bit embarrassed but amused, laughing and deciding to keep the socks anyway.

qa.q: Which part of Bhavna's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking the class to check what else happened on those days worked, because it let students discover other causes instead of just being told.

qa.q: How might the classmates who agreed with Ujjwal see the chart?
qa.a: They might feel surprised, and realise that seeing something happen together doesn't mean one thing caused the other.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher helping a teen tell a coincidence apart from a cause by looking for other factors.

passage:
Tuesday night
Diary, Vijay here. The news said kids who eat breakfast get better marks. Jaya, my sister, immediately said, "See? Breakfast makes you smart. Eat your poha."
I ate the poha (it was good). But then I thought: wait, who skips breakfast? In my class it's mostly the ones whose parents leave early for work, or who sleep late because they study till 2. Maybe they're just tired. Maybe breakfast and marks both come from having a calmer morning.
I said this to Jaya and she got annoyed: "It was on the news, Vijay." Being on the news doesn't prove which one causes which.
I still think breakfast is good. I just don't think the news proved what it said. I'm going to ask Sir tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the news say about breakfast?
qa.a: Kids who eat breakfast get better marks.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when Vijay questioned the news?
qa.a: Jaya felt annoyed, sure the news was right because it was on the news.

qa.q: What would you advise Vijay to ask Sir tomorrow?
qa.a: Vijay could ask how researchers tell whether breakfast causes better marks or whether both come from something else, like sleep or a calmer morning.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya read the study herself?
qa.a: Jaya might see what it actually measured and feel less certain, or find it did check for things like sleep.

grounding: Shows a teen questioning a news claim by thinking about other causes, not trusting it just because of its source.

passage:
In the small town of Sehore, a message was going round every family group: "Students who go to Verma Sir's tuition score 20 marks more! Enrol now!"
Chetan's mother read it aloud at dinner. "Everyone's joining. You should too."
Chetan, sixteen, put down his roti. "Ma, who goes to Verma Sir's?"
"The best students."
"Exactly. They were already scoring high before. And their parents can pay for extra books. The tuition might help, but the message doesn't prove it."
The next day at school, his friend Pradeep said, "My marks went up after I joined!"
"Did you also start studying more that month?"
Pradeep paused. "…Board exams were coming, so yes."
Chetan smiled. "So we don't know which one did it."

qa.q: How many more marks did the message say students would score?
qa.a: The message said they score 20 marks more.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he paused?
qa.a: Pradeep felt unsure and a bit surprised, realising his higher marks might have come from studying more, not only the tuition.

qa.q: What question could Chetan's mother ask before enrolling him?
qa.a: She could ask how students did before joining and compare with similar students who didn't join, to see if the tuition itself made the difference.

qa.q: How does Chetan's mother see the message compared with Chetan?
qa.a: She trusts it because everyone is joining, while Chetan sees that the best students were already scoring high, so the message proves nothing.

grounding: Shows a teenager separating correlation from causation when judging a popular claim.
